title: Review: Ressence Type 11 Watch Is A Thematic Restart For The Innovative Horology Brand | aBlogtoWatchReview: Ressence Type 11 Watch Is A Thematic Restart For The Innovative Horology Brand | aBlogtoWatch
text: Before I get into my review of the Ressence Type 11 wristwatch, I want to compliment the Ressence website for the depth and volume of the information it provides about its timepieces and the technology that goes into them. I often find myself puzzled at why luxury watch brands put in so little effort to fully articulate the value proposition of their products on their own websites. Routinely, I visit the websites of complicated, technically challenging watches that do not explain, discuss, or visually show nearly anything of actual importance to the deeper story of that product. Ressence, on the other hand, while not a big operation, has pretty well fleshed-out technical explanations, animated diagrams, and explanations of what goes into its watches and what they might be like to live with and wear. Unlike most watch websites that require you to be armed with most of the products’ context prior to visiting, the people behind Ressence have taken it upon themselves to educate and explain the brand’s technology to users. I see that as being a commitment to customer service that a lot of competitor brands entirely lack. For more of what I am talking about, you can visit the “Innovation” section of the Ressence website. Type 11 Context: Why It Took Two Decades For Ressence To Build The Watch Benoit Mintiens Always Wanted Now on to the Ressence Type 11 timepiece itself. This is a great product from Belgium-based Ressence, but it can be difficult to fully understand without some additional historical context about what I believe Benoit Mintiens (founder of Ressence) was trying to achieve with the Type 11. The succinct way of putting it is that I believe the Type 11 is the watch Ressence wanted to create from the very beginning. It took the brand about 20 years to achieve it, though. Much of what Ressence developed prior to the Type 11 was like a compromised evolutionary step along the way. That isn’t to say previous Ressence watches are bad or anything like that, but many of them they are innovation steps along the way to reaching something like what Ressence has achieved with the Type 11.Advertising Message Founder Benoit Mintiens is an industrial designer with a vision. He wanted a crownless watch with a particular rotating orbital convex display (which he eventually called ROCS, also knows as “Ressence Orbital Convex System”). What he learned early on was that if he wanted to execute his dream, he would need to design the system itself. Soon after, he also learned that if he wanted much of his watches to work as intended, he would also have to build or manufacture the parts himself. Ressence tried to find a compromise in previous watch models by using existing mechanical watch movements and modifying them, while creating bespoke modules on top of them that powered the signature ROCS display systems. Many of these are patented, and the Type 11 watch (accordingly) has the ROCS 11.1 display system. Building modules on top of existing systems, trying to connect them with magnets or through oil, just ended up making a lot of Ressence watches extra complicated while not necessarily offering a better ownership experience. The quest to make the Ressence watch that Mr. Mintiens truly wanted was also the quest to create an in-house-designed movement system that could power it. Why The In-House Caliber Werk RW-01 Automatic Movement Changes The Rules For What Ressence Can Build What Ressence debuted with the Type 11 watch is also its first exclusive “in-house” movement. Known as the Ressence caliber Werk RW-01, the movement is fully designed by Ressence to meet its particular requirements. The RW-01 automatic movement operates at 4Hz, with 60 hours of power reserve between two mainspring barrels. The movement fully integrates the ROCS display system, and as a result allows for a thinner profile and a more elegant internal mechanism. The visual architecture of the RW-01 is not the same as most other mechanical movements, and each movement is further individually serialized. One of the best things about the RW-01 movement is that it removes the odd way that many previous Ressence watches needed to be set. Since there isn’t a crown, things need to be done a bit differently. The RW-01 introduces a fold-out titanium metal winding handle. The handle system works well, but I worry about its durability. You need to hold it in the right way while turning, and without going too fast. I wonder if less cautious wearers end up breaking the handle, and if Ressence will need to create something thicker in the future for this part of the watch. These are just my various observations and suspicions. It might be that while the handle feels fragile, the titanium construction makes it tougher than it seems. Turn the handle one direction, and it adjusts the time forward. Turn the handle in the other direction, and you adjust the time backwards. There is nothing else to set. Also important to mention is that when the handle turns in one of the two directions, it winds the mainspring barrel for manual winding purposes. Yes, manually winding the watch will change the time, but then you just change the watch back to the correct time after you wind it. I suppose Ressence figures that, in today’s world, you’ll always have a mobile phone or other reference clock around in order to adjust the time on your Type 11 if necessary.Advertising Message ROCS 11.1 & The Novel Ceramic Bead Power Reserve Indicator Display Ressence points out that the Werk RW-01 movement has 40 jewels, 67 gears, and 18 ball bearings. It also has a number of small ceramic balls. One of the most interesting features of the RW-01 movement is the power reserve indicator. The dial looks complicated, but is merely a regulator-style display showing the hours, minutes (on the main turning disc), seconds, and a power reserve indicator. The power reserve indicator is not a new concept, but the particular method of how the display works is. In short, rather than a hand, disc, or arrow as an indicator, Ressence uses small colored ceramic beads. There is actually a small spiral graphic near the power reserve indicator, which is actually how the hidden part of the scale works (the ceramic spheres are stacked in a spiral-shaped cavity). The small beads are colored, and represent full or empty zones on the power reserve indicator. As the power winds up, the yellow ball moves clockwise and is followed by white balls that tend to fill out the scale with a light color as it gets full. As the power reserve in the movement recedes, the balls get pushed back, and the dark blue ceramic spheres take over. Honestly, the detail is hard for the naked eye to see (even though reading the indicator is clear enough), but the visual effect works, and I think it is a great approach to engineering a power reserve indicator in a product like this. The Type 11 dial is very legible and fully lumed as well. The overall surface area is convex, but the discs-within-discs ROCS display is otherwise flush. Most of it is produced from grade 5 titanium, just like the rest of the Type 11 case. At launch, Ressence offers three dial colors for the Type 11. They include the pictured “Sky” blue option, as well as a green “Pine” and tan “Latte” color. Given how important the Type 11 and Werk RW-01 movement are to the brand, I fully anticipate more Type 11 watch options in the future (probably meaning more dial colors). In any event, the Werk RW-01 movement will not only be produced for a number of more years, but I suspect Ressence will use it as a base to perhaps build additional complications or systems on top of. With that said, I can’t think of any other major features I’d like to see in a watch like the Ressence Type 11 that it does not already display, while keeping the package simple and approachable. Ergonomics & Legibility Of The Type 11’s 49 Gram Titanium Pebble Smooth Case On the wrist, the Ressence Type 11 case is produced from polished grade 5 titanium and is very light and comfortable. The Type 11 case is also quite attractive, with elegant lines and graceful curves. Ressence was, of course, inspired by a smooth pebble for the Type 11 case. Accordingly, it is very smooth to the touch without any sharp or snagging edges. The Type 11 case is 41mm wide by 11mm thick (with 30 meters of water resistance), but honestly feels thinner. The Type 11 watch is also very lightweight, being just 49 grams, with the strap included. That means it is easy to read and see the time, but when you aren’t looking at it, the Type 11 easily disappears from thought given its ergonomic comfort. Over the dial is a domed and AR-coated sapphire crystal. There is another small banana-shaped sapphire crystal window on the caseback, with a selective view of the movement just over where the balance wheel is placed. The sapphire crystal over the face has a fair bit of glare. Actually, it probably has less glare than most other Ressence watches, but that isn’t saying much. Photographing the Type 11 with a clear view of the dial is a challenge. Having said that, when you are living with the Type 11 and just trying to indicate the time, the glare really isn’t a problem at all. Aside from a high price, I don’t really have any complaints about the Ressence Type 11 other than the choice of strap and buckle. They are nice-looking for sure, but they present a bit of an ergonomic issue when putting the watch on. I also worry about the relatively flat buckle being fragile and scratching. It is titanium yes, but it is also pretty thin and flat. I might be over-worried, but it seems like a part like that needs to have a bit more durability in mind. The buckle isn’t my issue as much as the stickiness of the strap. In addition to the buckle having a section where excess strap tucks under, there are two ring loops on the strap to further tuck the excess strap. The soft leather is nice to touch, but it gets stuck on itself. So I find myself having to mess with it and tug it a lot when putting the watch on. That just isn’t ideal. If I owned this watches, one of the first things I’d probably do is swap out the included 20mm wide strap with something else that is a bit more practical (and keep the factory strap fresh and in the box). The Type 11 In Relation To Other Ressence Watches & Its Value Proposition Thin, easy to set, powered by an uncompromised mechanical engine, and elegantly presented, the Ressence Type 11 watch is really a summary of so much that Ressence has been working on over the years. I wouldn’t go so far as to say that the Type 11 invalidates other Ressence models, but it certainly makes others feel like stepping stones. Interestingly enough, the Type 11 is by no means the most expensive Ressence model the company makes, and is priced somewhere in the middle. There are other Ressence watches that cost nearly $20,000 USD more. Ressence Type 3, 5, and 7 watch models are typically more expensive, even though they have modular movements compared to the slick integrated RW-01. I suspect that Ressence will, over time, start to replace the movements in their other iconic watch models with RW-01-based systems. We will see. Ressence cannot really agree that the Type 11 watch is a thematic restart for the brand because it has other watch model families it is concurrently trying to push. I however, have been personally talking to Benoit Mintiens about his work for nearly 20 years, so I do understand what his challenges have been, where the brand has been, and what he has been striving for. He certainly isn’t done, but I think the in-house-designed RW-01 automatic movement and the Type 11 watches that house it are a real milestone for the luxury timepiece brand. Price for the titanium Ressence Type 11 watch is $31,400 USD. Learn more at the Ressence watch website. Watch Brand Ressence Tags Watch Releases 2026, Watch Reviews Over $500
